cards.front: Which step limits acetylcholine synthesis, and which drug blocks it?
cards.back: Uptake of choline into the axon by the Na+-choline cotransporter is the rate-limiting step; choline acetyltransferase then acetylates it. Hemicholinium blocks choline uptake and depletes ACh stores.

cards.front: Botulinum toxin: where and how does it act at cholinergic terminals?
cards.back: Botulinum toxins A and B are bacterial exotoxins whose active fragments are endopeptidases: they cleave SNARE proteins (e.g. synaptobrevin) needed for exocytosis, so ACh release fails and cholinergic transmission is lost for a long time. Local injection is used in blepharospasm, strabismus, spasmodic torticollis (cervical dystonia), spastic cerebral palsy and post-stroke spasticity, axillary hyperhidrosis, cosmetic removal of facial wrinkles, and (GG14) chronic migraine prophylaxis and overactive bladder. Wrong placement or overdose causes ptosis, diplopia and dysphagia. Black widow spider toxin (latrotoxin) does the opposite: massive ACh release, then depletion.

cards.front: Which G-protein pathways do the muscarinic receptor subtypes M1 to M5 use?
cards.back: M1, M3 and M5 couple through Gq: phospholipase C, IP3 and DAG, then intracellular Ca2+ release. M2 and M4 couple through Gi/Go: K+ channel opening and inhibition of adenylyl cyclase.

cards.front: Where are the NM and NN nicotinic receptors, and which agonists and blockers identify each?
cards.back: NM is at the skeletal muscle endplate: stimulated by PTMA, blocked by tubocurarine. NN is at autonomic ganglia (both divisions) and the adrenal medulla, and in the CNS: stimulated by DMPP, blocked by hexamethonium.

cards.front: Short note: Muscarinic receptor subtypes

points: M1, M3, M5: Gq, phospholipase C, IP3 and DAG, Ca2+ release
M2, M4: Gi/Go, K+ channel opening, reduced cAMP
Ganglion cells, enteric and central neurones
Gastric acid secretion, learning and memory
Heart: slows SA and AV nodes, reduces atrial force
Prejunctional autoreceptors inhibit ACh release

cards.front: Classify: muscarinic subtypes
cards.text: M1, M3 and M5 couple through {{Gq}}, while M2 and M4 couple through {{Gi/Go}}; M2 predominates in the {{heart}}, whereas M3 predominates in {{smooth muscle and glands}}.

cards.front: Classify: nicotinic receptor subtypes
cards.text: NM receptors at the {{skeletal muscle endplate}} are blocked by {{tubocurarine}}; NN receptors in {{autonomic ganglia}} are stimulated by {{DMPP}} and blocked by {{hexamethonium}}.

cards.front: What are the cardiac effects of acetylcholine acting on M2 receptors?
cards.back: It hyperpolarises SA nodal cells and slows the rate of diastolic depolarisation, causing bradycardia that can progress to arrest. It slows AV conduction and lengthens the AV nodal refractory period, which can produce PR prolongation or AV block. Atrial force falls and atrial refractoriness shortens; ventricular contractility falls only slightly.

cards.front: Short note: Acetylcholine as a clinical agent

points: Rarely given systemically; cholinesterase hydrolyses it quickly, so action is brief
1% solution instilled in the eye induces miosis during ophthalmic surgery
Carbachol (intraocular) and pilocarpine also used to produce miosis

cards.front: Essay: Acetylcholine - synthesis, receptors and actions

points: Choline uptake by Na+ cotransport (rate-limiting), ChAT, vesicular transporter
Released in quanta by exocytosis

cards.front: Pilocarpine: what is its main use and where does it fit in glaucoma therapy?
cards.back: A muscarinic agonist used as eye drops (0.5 to 4%). It causes miosis, ciliary muscle contraction and a fall in intraocular pressure. It is the preferred miotic, but miotics are third-line in open-angle glaucoma; it is also used in angle-closure glaucoma. Frequent side effects are brow pain and spasm of accommodation.

cards.front: Bethanechol: uses and adverse effects.
cards.back: A muscarinic agonist resistant to cholinesterase, used for non-obstructive urinary retention (postoperative or postpartum) and neurogenic bladder. Adverse effects include belching, colic, involuntary urination or defaecation, flushing, sweating, fall in BP and bronchospasm.

Used as eye drops for glaucoma and as a miotic; KDT notes no oral preparation is available, though it could be a sialogogue

cards.front: Classify: direct agonists versus anticholinesterases
cards.text: Direct cholinergic agonists include {{carbachol}}, {{bethanechol}} and {{pilocarpine}}; anticholinesterases include {{neostigmine}}, {{physostigmine}} and {{edrophonium}}.

cards.front: Why are the choline esters short-acting even though they resist cholinesterase?
cards.back: Even though they resist cholinesterase hydrolysis (carbachol and bethanechol almost completely), the choline esters are short-acting because of rapid renal elimination.

cards.front: What is the key difference of methacholine from ACh?
cards.back: It is longer acting: its added methyl group resists cholinesterase hydrolysis. Its actions are muscarinic-predominant, with minor nicotinic effects.

cards.front: Short note: Therapeutic uses of cholinergic (muscarinic) agonists, with rationale

points: Bethanechol stimulates the bladder and relieves retention without organic obstruction
Uses: postoperative retention, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, neurogenic bladder; avoids catheterisation
Bethanechol raises peristalsis and lower oesophageal sphincter pressure
Older uses (ileus, gastroparesis, reflux) now replaced by better drugs
Pilocarpine treats xerostomia after head and neck radiation or in Sjogren syndrome
Works only if salivary tissue retains residual function
Pilocarpine and carbachol cause miosis and lower IOP in glaucoma

cards.front: Classify: reversible anticholinesterases by chemistry
cards.text: Carbamates include {{neostigmine}}, {{physostigmine}}, {{pyridostigmine}} and {{rivastigmine}}; non-carbamates with carbamate-like action include {{edrophonium}}, {{tacrine}}, {{donepezil}} and {{galantamine}}.

cards.front: Which anticholinesterases are used in myasthenia gravis, and how do their durations differ?
cards.back: Neostigmine is the standard drug. Pyridostigmine is less potent dose for dose but longer acting, so it needs less frequent dosing; ambenonium is another long-acting congener. Edrophonium lasts only 10 to 30 minutes, so it is used only for diagnosis.

cards.front: What are the contraindications and cautions for anticholinesterase drugs?
cards.back: Contraindicated in sick sinus, AV conduction defects and hypotensive states, because accumulated ACh causes bradycardia and fall in cardiac output. Use cautiously in peptic ulcer, hypertension, asthma, COPD and seizure disorders.

cards.front: Compare true (acetylcholinesterase) and pseudo (butyrylcholinesterase) cholinesterase.
cards.back: AChE is at all cholinergic sites, in RBCs and grey matter; it hydrolyses ACh very rapidly to end its action and does not hydrolyse butyrylcholine. BuChE is in plasma, liver, intestine and white matter; it hydrolyses ACh slowly, hydrolyses butyrylcholine and ingested esters (and succinylcholine), and does not hydrolyse methacholine.

cards.front: Why do anticholinesterases differ in their CNS and neuromuscular actions?
cards.back: Lipid-soluble tertiary agents (physostigmine, organophosphates) cross into the CNS and have strong muscarinic and central effects. Quaternary agents (neostigmine and congeners) do not enter the CNS, have weak muscarinic effects, and act directly on NM receptors at the endplate.

cards.front: How does edrophonium's enzyme binding differ from an organophosphate's?
cards.back: Edrophonium binds only the anionic site through weak hydrogen bonds, with no covalent bond, so the enzyme recovers within minutes and the action is brief. Organophosphates bind the esteratic site covalently, phosphorylating it; recovery is very slow and the enzyme can age and become resistant to reactivation.

Physostigmine: miotic in glaucoma; antidote for central anticholinergic (belladonna) toxicity
Neostigmine: myasthenia gravis, decurarisation, postoperative ileus or urinary retention
Physostigmine: 6 to 24 h in the eye, 4 to 6 h systemically
Neostigmine: about 3 to 4 h

Edrophonium test for myasthenia; overdose causes cholinergic weakness

M2 and M5 involved in cognition in animal models
Systemic ACh has limited CNS entry; BBB-crossing muscarinic agonists give cortical arousal similar to cholinesterase inhibitors
Cholinesterase inhibitors raise brain ACh and are used in Alzheimer disease

cards.front: What is the basic defect in myasthenia gravis and why do anticholinesterases help?
cards.back: Autoantibodies against nicotinic receptors at the muscle endplate leave only about a third or fewer free receptors, causing weakness that worsens with repeated activity and recovers with rest. Anticholinesterases let released ACh persist and act on the remaining receptors repeatedly, restoring strength, but they do not treat the disease itself.

cards.front: How is myasthenia gravis treated first-line, and which drug controls the side effects?
cards.back: Neostigmine (about 15 mg orally 6-hourly, adjusted to response) or pyridostigmine, which needs less frequent dosing. Intolerable muscarinic effects are blocked by adding atropine. Needs fluctuate, with unpredictable remissions and relapses, so dose is individualised.

cards.front: How does the edrophonium test diagnose myasthenia gravis?
cards.back: Edrophonium 2 mg IV is given as a test dose, then 8 mg after 30 to 60 seconds if nothing untoward occurs. Brief reversal of weakness occurs in myasthenia but not in other muscular dystrophies. If edrophonium is unavailable, neostigmine 1.5 mg IV can be used, with atropine pretreatment.

cards.front: Short note: Immunotherapy and other measures beyond anticholinesterases in myasthenia gravis

points: Advised in generalised weakness, thymoma and younger patients; gradual improvement, even remission
Reduce antibody production, may increase new receptor synthesis; reserved for poor response to anti-ChEs or failed thymectomy; prednisolone induces remission in most advanced cases
Azathioprine (slow onset, good for maintenance) and cyclosporine inhibit antibody synthesis via T cells
Removes antibodies; dramatic but short-lived benefit, useful in crisis

cards.front: Compare the three diagnostic tests for myasthenia gravis and say which is most reliable.
cards.back: Ameliorative test (edrophonium): short-lived improvement. Provocative test: myasthenics are very sensitive to d-tubocurarine (0.5 mg IV causes marked weakness), but this is hazardous. Demonstration of anti-receptor antibodies in plasma or a muscle biopsy is the more reliable test.

cards.front: Short note: Myasthenic crisis versus cholinergic crisis

Tracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
IV methylprednisolone pulse while anti-ChEs are withheld for 2 to 3 days, then reintroduced gradually
Plasmapheresis hastens recovery; immunoglobulins help very severe disease (Katzung)
Relative overdose of anti-ChE causes persistent endplate depolarisation
Muscarinic features dominate: salivation, sweating, bradycardia, miosis, diarrhoea
Stop the anti-ChE and give atropine for muscarinic effects
Edrophonium 2 mg IV: improvement suggests myasthenic crisis
No improvement or worsening suggests cholinergic crisis
Should be done in hospital with ventilator support available
The two need opposite treatment
Late cases with high anti-ChE needs can alternate between the two

Neostigmine 1.5 mg IV (with atropine cover) can replace edrophonium

Azathioprine (slow onset, good for maintenance), cyclosporine; high-dose cyclophosphamide in refractory cases
Plasmapheresis and immunoglobulins for severe disease or crisis
Advised for generalised disease, thymoma and younger patients
Gradual improvement; remission possible

Curariform drugs, certain antibiotics and general anaesthetics impair neuromuscular transmission and need care in myasthenics

cards.front: Classify: mushroom poisoning types
cards.text: Early {{muscarine}}-type poisoning is due to {{Inocybe}} species and is reversed by {{atropine}}; the hallucinogenic type from {{Amanita muscaria}} is treated without atropine; the late {{phalloidin}} type damages the {{gut, liver and kidney}}.

cards.front: What does atropine achieve in anticholinesterase poisoning, and how is it dosed?
cards.back: It counters the muscarinic features, but needs higher doses for central effects and does not reverse nicotinic muscle paralysis. Give 2 mg IV, repeated every 10 minutes until atropinisation (dry mouth); maintenance may be needed for 1 to 2 weeks. It is given in every carbamate or organophosphate case.

cards.front: List the general measures in anticholinesterase poisoning before specific antidotes.
cards.back: Stop exposure (fresh air, wash skin and mucosa with soap and water, lavage as needed), keep the airway open and ventilate if breathing fails, support BP and hydration, and control convulsions carefully with diazepam. Death is usually from respiratory failure, so airway comes first.

cards.front: Why is pralidoxime used in organophosphate poisoning but contraindicated in carbamate poisoning?
cards.back: Pralidoxime's quaternary nitrogen binds the anionic site, which the organophosphate leaves free, and its oxime end attacks the phosphorus on the esteratic site; the oxime-phosphonate diffuses away and the enzyme is reactivated (only before ageing). In carbamate poisoning the anionic site is not free, the carbamylated enzyme is not reactivated, and pralidoxime's own weak anti-ChE activity can add to toxicity, so it is not recommended (KDT: contraindicated).

cards.front: Which mushroom poisonings are reversed by atropine, and which are not?
cards.back: Early muscarine-type poisoning (Inocybe species) gives muscarinic signs within an hour and is promptly reversed by atropine. The hallucinogenic type (Amanita muscaria, due to muscimol) has no specific treatment and atropine is contraindicated. The late phalloidin type (Amanita phalloides) damages the gut, liver and kidney and is managed supportively.

cards.front: Short note: Organophosphate (anticholinesterase) poisoning

Systemic muscarinic signs: bronchospasm, bronchorrhoea, colic, defaecation, micturition
Nicotinic: fasciculations, weakness, respiratory paralysis
CNS: confusion, convulsions, coma; death usually from respiratory failure
Stop exposure, wash skin, lavage if ingested
Secure airway; ventilate if failing; maintain BP and hydration
Diazepam for convulsions
Give early; it antagonises muscarinic effects (secretions, bronchoconstriction, bradycardia) but not nicotinic weakness; larger doses are needed for CNS effects
KDT: 2 mg IV every 10 min until signs of atropinisation (dry mouth); up to 200 mg has been needed in a day; maintenance may be required for 1 to 2 weeks
GG14: 2 to 4 mg IV first, then 2 mg every 5 to 10 min until muscarinic signs subside or atropine toxicity appears
Pralidoxime 1 to 2 g IV slowly (children 20 to 40 mg/kg); repeat if weakness persists or recurs after 20 to 60 min (GG14)
Alternative regimen (KDT): 30 mg/kg IV loading dose, then 8 to 10 mg/kg/h infusion until recovery
Start early, before the phosphorylated enzyme ages; works for organophosphates, not carbamates
Reactivates skeletal muscle ChE best; does not enter the brain; an adjunct to atropine, not a substitute
Intermediate syndrome: 1 to 4 days after exposure; persistent low ChE with severe muscle weakness from failing neuromuscular transmission; respiratory muscle weakness can be fatal
OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy: some fluorinated and triaryl organophosphates inhibit neuropathy target (neurotoxic) esterase; sensory symptoms then weakness after 1 to 2 weeks
The delayed neuropathy is not due to AChE inhibition and has no specific treatment

cards.front: What is the intermediate syndrome in organophosphate poisoning, and how does it differ from delayed neuropathy?
cards.back: It appears 1 to 4 days after exposure in severe poisoning: ChE stays low and severe muscle weakness develops from failing neuromuscular transmission, with nicotinic rather than muscarinic features. Respiratory muscle weakness can progress to death. OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy is different: it follows some fluorinated or triaryl compounds after 1 to 2 weeks, is due to inhibition of neuropathy target esterase rather than AChE, and causes sensory disturbance then limb weakness.

cards.front: Short note: Role of oximes in anticholinesterase poisoning

points: Phosphorylated ChE hydrolyses extremely slowly; an oxime group reactivates it over a million times faster
Quaternary N of pralidoxime binds the free anionic site; oxime end attacks phosphorus; oxime-phosphonate leaves, enzyme freed
Must be early, before aging; benefit varies with compound, amount and dose; acts more at muscle than autonomic sites, not in CNS; adjunct to atropine
Anionic site is occupied; pralidoxime has weak anti-ChE action of its own
Obidoxime (more potent); diacetyl-monoxime (lipophilic)

cards.front: What is delayed organophosphate neuropathy and why does atropine or an oxime not prevent it?
cards.back: Certain fluorine-containing and triaryl organophosphates cause polyneuritis and demyelination after days to weeks: sensory disturbance, then lower motor neurone weakness, later spastic upper motor neurone paralysis. It is not due to cholinesterase inhibition, so enzyme-directed antidotes do nothing; there is no specific treatment and recovery can take years.

cards.front: Essay: Management of organophosphorus poisoning

points: Easily available insecticides; accidental, suicidal and homicidal poisoning common
Phosphorylation of the esteratic site of cholinesterase amplifies ACh at muscarinic, nicotinic and central sites
Local then systemic muscarinic signs: lacrimation, salivation, sweating, secretions, miosis, bronchospasm, colic
Nicotinic: fasciculations, weakness, respiratory paralysis
CNS: irritability, convulsions, coma; death from respiratory failure
Stop exposure, decontaminate skin, lavage if ingested
Secure airway and ventilate; support BP; diazepam for convulsions
Primary antidote for muscarinic signs; 2 mg IV every 10 min until atropinisation
Does not reverse muscle paralysis
Pralidoxime reactivates phosphorylated enzyme only if given early, before aging
Weak in CNS (does not enter brain); adjunct to atropine
Useless and contraindicated in carbamate poisoning
Some fluorine-containing and triaryl OPs cause delayed polyneuritis not due to ChE inhibition; no specific treatment

cards.front: What kind of antagonist is atropine, and how does its selectivity change with dose?
cards.back: It is a competitive antagonist at muscarinic receptors and blocks all muscarinic subtypes. It is selective for muscarinic receptors at usual doses, but this selectivity is lost at very high doses.

cards.front: Atropine's central effects at low and high doses.
cards.back: Low doses have little central effect because brain entry is restricted, though atropine suppresses vestibular excitation (motion sickness) and reduces tremor and rigidity in parkinsonism by blocking relative cholinergic overactivity in the basal ganglia. High doses cause cortical excitation, restlessness, hallucinations and delirium, then respiratory depression and coma.

cards.front: What are the ocular effects of topical atropine, and what is the risk?
cards.back: Mydriasis, loss of the light reflex and cycloplegia lasting about 7 to 10 days, causing photophobia and blurred near vision. The ciliary muscle recovers before the sphincter pupillae. It can raise intraocular pressure and is dangerous in narrow-angle glaucoma.

cards.front: Rank the organs in order of sensitivity to atropine.
cards.back: Most sensitive: saliva, sweat and bronchial secretions. Next: eye, bronchial muscle and heart. Less sensitive: intestinal and bladder smooth muscle. Least sensitive: gastric glands and gastric smooth muscle. The pattern reflects how much each function depends on cholinergic tone.

cards.front: Atropine pharmacokinetics: how is it cleared, and what is its half-life?
cards.back: About half is metabolised in the liver and the rest is excreted unchanged in urine. The half-life is about 3 to 4 hours. Passage across the BBB is somewhat restricted.

cards.front: Name the contraindication and the caution for atropinic drugs.
cards.back: Absolute contraindication: narrow iridocorneal angle, because it can precipitate acute congestive glaucoma. Caution: elderly men with prostatic hypertrophy, in whom urinary retention can occur.

cards.front: Classify: mydriatics by onset and duration
cards.text: {{Tropicamide}} acts in {{20 to 40 min}} and lasts {{3 to 6 hours}}; {{cyclopentolate}} acts in {{30 to 60 min}} and lasts about {{one day}}; {{homatropine}} is about {{10 times}} less potent than atropine.

cards.front: What is atropine flush and why does it occur?
cards.back: Dilation of cutaneous vessels in the blush area, seen with toxic and sometimes therapeutic atropine doses. It is thought to be a compensatory heat-loss response to the rise in body temperature caused by suppressed sweating.

cards.front: Why does atropine cause tachycardia, and why does the effect vary between patients?
cards.back: It blocks M2 receptors on the SA node, removing vagal slowing. The rise depends on the existing vagal tone, so it is greatest in young adults and smaller in children and the elderly. Small IM/SC doses can first cause a transient bradycardia, now attributed to block of prejunctional M1 autoreceptors on vagal endings, which increases ACh release.

cards.front: What is the antidote for belladonna poisoning, and why is it a last resort?
cards.back: Physostigmine, 0.5 to 2 mg IV repeated as required. It crosses the BBB and reverses central and peripheral effects, but it can cause hypotension and arrhythmias, so it is used only as a last resort. Neostigmine does not reverse central effects. A useful bedside test: methacholine 5 mg or neostigmine 1 mg s.c. fails to produce muscarinic effects in an atropinised patient.

cards.front: Short note: Adverse effects and poisoning with atropine

points: Dry mouth, difficulty swallowing and talking
Dry, flushed, hot skin; fever; decreased bowel sounds
Urinary difficulty; dilated pupils, photophobia, blurred near vision
Palpitation
Excitement, psychotic behaviour, ataxia, delirium, visual hallucinations
Hypotension, weak rapid pulse, cardiovascular collapse, respiratory depression
Convulsions and coma occur only in severe cases
Children are highly susceptible
Gastric lavage with tannic acid (potassium permanganate is ineffective)
Dark, quiet room; cold sponging or ice bags for fever
Diazepam for convulsions; maintain blood volume and assist respiration
Physostigmine only as a last resort

points: Preanaesthetic medication, mainly with irritant anaesthetics and to block vasovagal attacks

Reduces secretions in pulmonary embolism; controls sweating or salivation in parkinsonism
Intestinal and renal colic, abdominal cramps, if no mechanical obstruction

Biliary colic: nitrates are more effective
Dysmenorrhoea: NSAIDs are superior

cards.front: Short note: Mydriatics and cycloplegics

points: Potent but slow; mydriasis and cycloplegia last days, so it is poor for refraction
Therapeutic use in iritis, keratitis and corneal ulcer, with analgesic and rest effects
Preferred for children below 5 years: 1% ointment applied 24 h and 2 h before
Tropicamide: acts in 20 to 40 min, lasts 3 to 6 h; relatively unreliable cycloplegic; augmented with phenylephrine
Cyclopentolate: acts in 30 to 60 min, lasts about a day; preferred for cycloplegic refraction; transient behaviour changes in children
Homatropine: about 10 times less potent than atropine; poor cycloplegia in children
Only mydriasis needed
Phenylephrine preferred in the elderly to avoid precipitating glaucoma

cards.front: Short note: Atropine versus scopolamine

points: Atropine (D,L-hyoscyamine) from Datura stramonium and belladonna
Scopolamine (L-hyoscine) mainly from Hyoscyamus niger (henbane)
Conventional systemic atropine has little ocular effect; equal scopolamine doses cause clear mydriasis and loss of accommodation
Topical atropine effects last 7 to 12 days; shorter agents such as homatropine and tropicamide are preferred as mydriatics
Pilocarpine and carbachol reverse the ocular effects of atropine

cards.front: Essay: Atropine - pharmacology, uses and toxicity

points: Prototype muscarinic antagonist from Solanaceae plants
Racemic; levo-isomers are more active; scopolamine is l-hyoscine
CNS: stimulant at low dose; delirium at high dose; antimotion sickness
Heart: tachycardia from M2 blockade; no consistent BP change
Eye: mydriasis, cycloplegia, raised pressure in narrow angle
Gut, bronchi, bladder: relaxation; less peristalsis and bronchial resistance
Glands: markedly reduced sweat, saliva, tracheobronchial and lacrimal secretion
Premedication, antispasmodic, mydriatic, cardiac vagolytic
Parkinsonism and drug-induced extrapyramidal syndromes (adjuvant)
Antidote for anti-ChE and early mushroom poisoning
Dry mouth, flushing, hyperthermia, urinary retention, blurred vision
Delirium, hallucinations, hypotension and collapse in severe cases
Narrow-angle glaucoma absolutely; caution in prostatic hypertrophy
Additive with TCAs, antihistamines, phenothiazines, disopyramide
Delays gastric emptying: reduces levodopa absorption; antacids reduce absorption
Gastric lavage with tannic acid; cool dark room; diazepam
Physostigmine last resort; neostigmine does not treat central effects

cards.front: Short note: Structure-activity relationships of atropine-type antimuscarinics

points: Intact ester of tropine and tropic acid is essential
Free acid and basic alcohol are inactive
Free OH in the acyl part is important for activity
More potent parenterally at muscarinic and ganglionic sites
Poorly and unreliably absorbed orally
Atropine has no subtype selectivity; most clinical antagonists act like atropine

cards.front: Short note: Why atropine can fail to speed the heart

points: Atropine removes vagal tone; the effect depends on how much tone is present
Young adults have high vagal tone; infants, elderly and heart failure patients may not respond even to large doses
Atropine abolishes reflex bradycardia from carotid sinus pressure, eyeball pressure, irritant vapours and contrast dye
Shortens AV node refractory period; can speed ventricle in atrial fibrillation or flutter
May lessen Wenckebach block from digoxin toxicity

cards.front: Short note: Paradoxical responses to muscarinic antagonists

points: Muscarinic receptors on postganglionic parasympathetic terminals regulate release
Blocking them increases transmitter release, partly offsetting postsynaptic block
Blocking modulatory muscarinic receptors in ganglia gives additional paradoxical effects
Predicting drug action from receptor physiology sometimes fails; organ sensitivity varies

cards.front: Classify: quaternary antimuscarinics and their uses
cards.text: Quaternary antimuscarinics such as {{ipratropium}} and {{tiotropium}} are given by {{inhalation}} for {{COPD}} and asthma; {{glycopyrrolate}} is used as {{preanaesthetic}} medication; {{cimetropium}} is an antispasmodic for IBS.

cards.front: Classify: tertiary and vasicoselective antimuscarinics
cards.text: {{Dicyclomine}} is a tertiary amine with direct smooth muscle relaxant action; {{oxybutynin}} and {{flavoxate}} are {{vasicoselective}} agents for the bladder; {{tolterodine}} is relatively {{M3}}-selective.

cards.front: Classify: drugs with incidental antimuscarinic action
cards.text: Antimuscarinic side effects are seen with {{tricyclic antidepressants}}, {{phenothiazines}}, {{antihistaminics}}, {{disopyramide}} and {{pethidine}}, which can add to atropinic effects.

cards.front: How does hyoscine differ from atropine?
cards.back: Hyoscine (l-hyoscine, scopolamine) is more potent on the eye and secretory glands and has better anti-motion sickness action. It is a central depressant even at low doses, penetrates the BBB better, is more completely metabolised, and acts for a shorter time than atropine.

cards.front: How does inhaled ipratropium differ from atropine in airway use?
cards.back: It acts mainly on the larger central airways and does not dry secretions or impair mucociliary clearance. Its onset is gradual, with peak effect at 40 to 60 minutes and duration of 4 to 6 hours. It suits regular prophylaxis rather than rescue. It works better in COPD than asthma, and is combined with a beta-2 agonist in acute exacerbations.

cards.front: Why is tiotropium suited to once-daily maintenance in COPD?
cards.back: It binds M1 and M3 bronchial receptors very tightly and binds M2 less tightly. This gives long-lasting bronchodilatation for once-daily use, and M2 sparing avoids enhanced acetylcholine release from vagal nerve endings. Regular use reduces COPD exacerbations.

cards.front: Why is hyoscine the preferred drug for motion sickness, and how is it given?
cards.back: It is the most effective antimotion sickness antimuscarinic and works best when given prophylactically: 0.2 mg orally, or a transdermal patch behind the pinna about 4 hours before travel, which protects for up to 3 days. Dry mouth and sedation can occur, so driving is risky.

cards.front: Short note: Atropine substitutes

points: Relatively selective muscarinic antagonists that can replace atropine
Examples in KDT8: pirenzepine and telenzepine (M1-selective), methoctramine, tripitramine, solifenacin, darifenacin
Pirenzepine is equipotent to atropine in causing bradycardia
Substitutes that do not cross the blood-brain barrier still produce initial bradycardia

cards.front: Why do quaternary antimuscarinics such as ipratropium and tiotropium not cause CNS effects?
cards.back: They are quaternary amines that do not cross the blood-brain barrier or readily cross membranes. Inhaled absorption is inefficient, so systemic effects are small.

cards.front: Short note: Non-ocular therapeutic uses of anticholinergic drugs

points: Asthma and COPD bronchodilation (inhaled ipratropium, tiotropium)
Atropine dries airway secretions; prevented secretions with diethyl ether anaesthesia
Rhinorrhoea of colds and rhinitis
Pre-anaesthetic drying of secretions
Atropine or glycopyrrolate used to block neostigmine's muscarinic effects
Relieves vagal bradycardia, asystole and AV block; may help inferior MI bradycardia
Reduces salivary secretion, gut motility and urination at larger doses

cards.front: Short note: Vasicoselective antimuscarinics for overactive bladder

points: Act mainly on the bladder, with less effect on salivary glands and the heart
Used for detrusor instability, urgency, frequency and urge incontinence
Oxybutynin: M1/M3 antagonist with direct smooth muscle relaxant and local anaesthetic action; high incidence of antimuscarinic effects
Tolterodine: relatively M3 selective with preferential bladder action, less dry mouth
Darifenacin and solifenacin: some M3 preference, similar to each other
Trospium: quaternary, fewer CNS effects, mainly renally eliminated
Flavoxate: for frequency, urgency and dysuria with lower urinary tract infection
Dry mouth is the commonest reason for stopping; CNS effects trouble the elderly
Intravesical oxybutynin increases capacity with few side effects
CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels; reduce dose of oxybutynin and tolterodine
Non-antimuscarinic options (GG14): beta-3 agonists mirabegron and vibegron; onabotulinumtoxinA for overactive bladder

cards.front: Essay: Classification of atropine substitutes

points: Semisynthetic and synthetic analogues seek selectivity
Most differ only marginally from natural alkaloids
Poor oral absorption, poor CNS and eye penetration
Longer acting than atropine; more nicotinic blockade
Ganglion block causes postural hypotension and impotence at clinical doses
Hyoscine butyl bromide (less potent, longer acting), clidinium, cimetropium, oxyphenonium
Propantheline: once popular for peptic ulcer, now declined
Dicyclomine: direct smooth muscle relaxant with weak M1-selective action
Valethamate: hastens cervical dilatation in labour
Pirenzepine: selective M1 antagonist that inhibits gastric secretion
Oxybutynin, tolterodine, flavoxate, darifenacin, solifenacin for the bladder
Ipratropium and tiotropium for the airway
Drotaverine: PDE-4 inhibitor, smooth muscle antispasmodic without antimuscarinic side effects

cards.front: Short note: Selectivity of muscarinic antagonists and their receptor-subtype targets

points: Atropine, scopolamine and most clinical antagonists act like atropine
Pirenzepine: M1-preferring antagonist
Darifenacin and solifenacin: M3-preferring antagonists, once-daily because of long half-lives
Clinical efficacy of some agents depends on blocking two or more subtypes

cards.front: Classify: ganglion blockers and nicotinic agents
cards.text: {{Trimethaphan}} is an ultrashort-acting ganglion blocker given IV; {{varenicline}} is a partial agonist at the {{alpha4-beta2}} nicotinic receptor; {{bupropion}} inhibits reuptake of {{dopamine and noradrenaline}}.

cards.front: What does nicotine do at nicotinic receptors, and what is its only clinical use?
cards.back: It is an agonist at both NN and NM receptors; it stimulates sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, and larger doses cause persistent depolarisation and ganglionic blockade. Its only use is short-term replacement therapy in tobacco-abstinent people; stimulating both ganglion divisions together has no therapeutic value.

cards.front: Name the competitive ganglion blockers and their present status.
cards.back: Hexamethonium, trimethaphan and mecamylamine. Once used for hypertension and peptic ulcer, they were replaced because of intolerable side effects and none is marketed now. Trimethaphan was an ultrashort-acting infusion for controlled hypotension (aortic dissection); mecamylamine was tried for smoking cessation.

cards.front: Why do quaternary antimuscarinics carry a higher risk of ganglion and neuromuscular blockade?
cards.back: Quaternary ammonium antagonists generally show more nicotinic-blocking activity than tertiary antagonists, so they are more likely to interfere with ganglionic or neuromuscular transmission.

cards.front: Predict the side effects of ganglionic blockade from the dominant autonomic tone of each organ.
cards.back: Parasympathetic-dominant organs lose tone: tachycardia, mydriasis, cycloplegia, reduced gut motility (constipation), bladder atony. Sympathetic-dominant vessels dilate, giving postural hypotension and syncope; erection and ejaculation are inhibited. This explains why the drugs were abandoned.

cards.front: Compare nicotine patch, varenicline and bupropion for smoking cessation.
cards.back: Patch: replaces nicotine, eases withdrawal but only partly craving because the intermittent peaks of smoking are missing; avoid in arrhythmia or ischaemic heart disease. Varenicline: alpha4beta2 partial agonist, gives some substitution while blocking reward; limited by mood changes and suicidal-thought warning. Bupropion: blocks DA and NA reuptake, equal efficacy with fewer side effects.

cards.front: Short note: Nicotine and pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation

points: Principal tobacco alkaloid; agonist at both NN and NM receptors
Low doses stimulate ganglia; high doses cause persistent depolarisation and block
Clinical use limited to short-term replacement therapy
Forms: transdermal patch, chewing gum, lozenge, nasal spray, inhaler
Gum 2 or 4 mg (4 mg for heavy smokers), used when the urge arises
Side effects: headache, dyspepsia, insomnia, local irritation
KDT: contraindicated in arrhythmias and ischaemic heart disease
Partial agonist at alpha4-beta2 nicotinic receptors: partly substitutes for nicotine and blocks its reward
GG14 dosing: 0.5 mg once daily for 3 days, then twice daily, then 1 mg twice daily from day 8; KDT limits the course to 12 weeks
More effective than placebo, nicotine patch or bupropion; NRT plus varenicline gives the highest quit rates
Older suicidal-thought warning was revised down in 2016 after newer studies; still monitor mood and behaviour
Bupropion: inhibits dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake; lowers seizure threshold
Cytisine: plant alkaloid, alpha4-beta2 partial agonist, appears effective (not approved in US/Europe)
Counselling and behavioural support add to any drug

cards.front: Essay: Drugs acting on autonomic ganglia

points: ACh is the main excitatory transmitter; NN receptors give rapid depolarisation
Slow modulation by muscarinic M1 and M2, adrenergic, dopaminergic and peptidergic receptors
Ganglion is a complex integrating system, not a simple relay
Agonist at NN and NM; stimulates both divisions at low doses
Persistent depolarisation and blockade at high doses
No therapeutic role as a ganglion stimulant
Hexamethonium, trimethaphan (ultrashort, IV), mecamylamine
Effects: tachycardia, vasodilatation with postural hypotension, mydriasis, cycloplegia
Reduced gut motility, urinary retention, impotence, dry mouth, anhidrosis
Replaced by safer drugs after use in hypertension and peptic ulcer in the 1950s
Trimethaphan used IV for controlled hypotension
Mecamylamine tested for smoking cessation
Ganglion blockade effects reveal the dominant tone of each organ

cards.front: What is Alzheimer's disease, and what is its cholinergic defect?
cards.back: A progressive neurodegenerative dementia of older people, with amyloid plaques and tau tangles. Brain cholinergic transmission is markedly deficient.

cards.front: Why is donepezil given once daily at bedtime?
cards.back: Its half-life is about 70 hours. Rivastigmine and galantamine have shorter half-lives and need twice-daily dosing.

cards.front: How does memantine act in Alzheimer's disease?
cards.back: It blocks NMDA-type glutamate receptors in a use-dependent way, limiting glutamate excitotoxicity. It is not a cholinesterase inhibitor.

cards.front: Why was tacrine withdrawn from Alzheimer's therapy?
cards.back: It was the first centrally acting anticholinesterase for AD, but caused hepatotoxicity (raised alanine aminotransferase), so its use fell away.

cards.front: Compare donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine in Alzheimer's disease.
cards.back: Donepezil: reversible, cerebroselective AChE inhibitor, once daily. Rivastigmine: lipophilic carbamate inhibiting AChE and BuChE, also available as a patch. Galantamine: natural alkaloid, selective for cerebral AChE, with some direct nicotinic agonism, twice daily. All three give similar modest benefit.

cards.front: What is the cholinergic hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease?
cards.back: Acetylcholine deficiency is critical to the symptoms. Support: the ACh deficit is selective, and central antagonists such as atropine can cause a confusional state resembling AD. AD also involves glutamate, 5HT and neuropeptide systems.

cards.front: What are the main adverse effects of cholinesterase inhibitors in AD?
cards.back: GI upset (diarrhoea, anorexia, nausea), muscle pain, weird dreams, fatigue, insomnia and hallucinations. GI effects are the main dose-limiting side effect; bradycardia and syncope are less common.

cards.front: When is memantine used instead of a cholinesterase inhibitor in AD?
cards.back: Memantine is indicated for moderate-to-severe dementia, as evidence in earlier stages is weak. It may replace or supplement cholinesterase inhibitors, which are used in mild or moderate AD.

cards.front: Essay: Role of cholinesterase activity in nervous and mental disorders

points: AChE hydrolyses ACh at cholinergic sites, inactivating it rapidly
BuChE (pseudocholinesterase) is a second, nonspecific enzyme
Progressive dementia with amyloid plaques and tau tangles
Marked fall in brain ACh and loss of cholinergic neurones: the cholinergic hypothesis
Confusion resembling AD follows central antagonists such as atropine
Lipophilic anticholinesterases enter the brain and cause a generalised alerting response
Higher doses cause excitement, confusion, disorientation, tremor, convulsions, then coma
Physostigmine reverses atropine intoxication and anticholinergic delirium
Rivastigmine, donepezil and galantamine are the cerebroselective agents used in AD
Tacrine was withdrawn for hepatotoxicity
Antipsychotics with strong antimuscarinic action (thioridazine highest) cause dry mouth and constipation
Thioridazine has the highest anticholinergic propensity among antipsychotics

cards.front: Essay: Neurotransmitter dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease; value and limitations of drugs

points: Cholinergic deficit is the most striking defect: atrophy of subcortical cholinergic neurones
Glutamate, 5HT and neuropeptide systems are also affected
Amyloid and tau pathology drive neuronal damage
Rivastigmine, donepezil and galantamine augment cholinergic transmission
Produce modest symptomatic benefit in about half of mild-to-moderate patients
Slow decline for a time but do not prevent it; stop if no benefit in about 3 months
NMDA antagonist for moderate-to-severe AD, given alone or with a cholinesterase inhibitor
Better tolerated than cholinesterase inhibitors
GI, muscle and sleep adverse effects; bradycardia and syncope are less common (GG14)
GI, muscle and sleep adverse effects; caution with bradycardia
Tacrine hepatotoxicity; benefit is limited and short-lasting
Anti-amyloid antibody aducanumab reduces plaques and is FDA approved; clinical efficacy uncertain (GG14)
Used alongside symptomatic drugs

cards.front: What is a spasmolytic (antispasmodic)?
cards.back: A drug that relieves spasm of smooth muscle (gut, bladder, biliary tract) or of skeletal muscle in spasticity, easing colic and spasm pain. Gut antispasmodics include antimuscarinics such as atropine, glycopyrrolate and dicyclomine, plus non-anticholinergic drotaverine.

cards.front: Why is glycopyrrolate preferred when central effects must be avoided?
cards.back: It is a potent, rapidly acting antimuscarinic that lacks central effects, unlike atropine (CNS stimulation) and hyoscine (central depression).

cards.front: What is dicyclomine's action on the gut?
cards.back: A weak muscarinic antagonist with a direct, nonspecific spasmolytic effect on GI smooth muscle. Occasionally used for diarrhoea-predominant IBS.

cards.front: Where does dantrolene act?
cards.back: On RyR1 calcium release channels of the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum. It blocks the Ca2+ release that couples excitation to contraction, without affecting neuromuscular transmission.

cards.front: How does baclofen work?
cards.back: A selective GABA-B agonist that acts mainly in the spinal cord, decreasing transmitter release and depressing mono- and polysynaptic reflexes. It causes some weakness and is less sedating than diazepam.

cards.front: How does botulinum toxin reduce muscle contraction?
cards.back: It causes long-lasting loss of cholinergic transmission by interfering with exocytotic release of ACh at the nerve ending. Localised injection treats focal spasms.

cards.front: Compare antimuscarinic and non-anticholinergic antispasmodics.
cards.back: Antimuscarinics (atropine methonitrate, clidinium, cimetropium, glycopyrrolate) block muscarinic receptors and so cause dry mouth and other antimuscarinic effects. Drotaverine is a non-anticholinergic smooth muscle antispasmodic, so it lacks these effects.

cards.front: Where is atropine least useful as an antispasmodic?
cards.back: In biliary colic and biliary spasm induced by opioids. In renal colic, parenteral opioids and NSAIDs relieve pain better; anticholinergics do not help infective diarrhoea.

cards.front: Which relaxant suits spinal spasticity, and why?
cards.back: Baclofen, for MS, ALS and spinal injury, because it is less sedative than diazepam. Dantrolene's weakness limits it to bedridden patients, and diazepam works through benzodiazepine receptors that enhance GABA transmission.

cards.front: Essay: Spasmolytics

points: Drugs that relieve smooth or skeletal muscle spasm
Smooth muscle: gut, biliary tract, ureter, bladder; skeletal muscle: spasticity and painful spasm
Atropine: intestinal and renal colic, nervous or drug-induced diarrhoea; not in infective diarrhoea
Clidinium with benzodiazepine; cimetropium quaternary agent for IBS; dicyclomine; glycopyrrolate (no central effects)
Adverse effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention
Drotaverine: smooth muscle antispasmodic without anticholinergic effects
Baclofen: GABA-B agonist, spinal, preferred in spasticity
Diazepam: benzodiazepine, enhances GABA transmission, sedating
Dantrolene: RyR1 blocker, muscle weakness limits use; drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia
Botulinum toxin: blocks ACh release, focal spasms
Atropine less effective in biliary colic; not for infective diarrhoea
Mephenesin not used clinically (gastric irritation, thrombophlebitis)

cards.front: What is malathion, and why is it less toxic to mammals than parathion?
cards.back: An organophosphate insecticide (thionophosphate) that is a prodrug: it must be converted to malaoxon. Plasma carboxylesterases hydrolyse it quickly, giving a wider safety margin than parathion.

cards.front: Short note: Malathion poisoning

points: Largely agricultural organophosphate insecticide
Thionophosphate prodrug; malaoxon is the active anti-cholinesterase metabolite
Mammalian lethal dose about 1 g/kg
Same muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS pattern as other organophosphates
Generally less toxic than parathion because of carboxylesterase detoxification
Atropine for muscarinic signs; oxime and anticonvulsant as for organophosphate poisoning in general
Reactivation fails once the enzyme has aged
Topical treatment of head lice where permethrin resistance exists

cards.front: Short note: Autonomic neurotransmitters

points: ACh at preganglionic fibres of both divisions and at postganglionic parasympathetic fibres
ACh at sympathetic postganglionic fibres to sweat glands and some vessels
ACh acts on nicotinic receptors of the adrenal medulla, releasing adrenaline and noradrenaline
Noradrenaline is the principal transmitter of postganglionic sympathetic nerves
ACh released in quanta by exocytosis
Cotransmitters are stored separately from the primary transmitter and released together
ATP: initial short phase of a biphasic vascular response (P2 receptors)
VIP: slow, long-lasting response
Nitric oxide: intermediate time course, between VIP and ACh
NPY: slower acting than noradrenaline

cards.front: Short note: Limitations of pharmacotherapy in myasthenia gravis

points: Anti-cholinesterases improve neuromuscular transmission but do not alter the autoimmune disease
Needs fluctuate, with unpredictable remissions and relapses; dose is individualised
Muscarinic effects limit the dose; atropine or glycopyrrolate needed
Relative overdose causes cholinergic weakness (cholinergic crisis)
Azathioprine has a slow onset
Plasmapheresis benefit is short-lived
